paragraphs.heading: What physics studies
paragraphs.text: Physics is the science of matter and its most basic parts, of how matter moves and behaves in space and time, and of energy and force. It is among the most fundamental of the sciences, and a person who works in it is called a physicist. Its edges are not sharp. It overlaps with fields such as biophysics and quantum chemistry.

paragraphs.heading: An old subject with a Greek name
paragraphs.text: Physics is also one of the oldest subjects of study. Its name comes from the Latin physica, meaning the study of nature, borrowed from a Greek word for natural science. For most of the last two thousand years, physics, chemistry, biology and parts of mathematics were bundled together as natural philosophy. They split into separate fields during the Scientific Revolution of the 17th century. Physics became a science of its own when early modern Europeans used experiments and measurement to find what we now call its laws.

paragraphs.heading: Greek beginnings
paragraphs.text: Natural philosophy began in Greece in the Archaic period, from 650 to 480 BCE. Thinkers such as Thales turned away from explanations outside nature and held that every event has a natural cause. Some of their ideas held up well: atomism, put forward by Leucippus and his pupil Democritus, proved right about 2000 years later. In the 4th century BC Aristotle wrote a long work called Physics. He mixed some observation with logical argument but did not test his conclusions by experiment, and his approach has since been entirely replaced.

paragraphs.heading: Aristotle's ordered world
paragraphs.text: Aristotle's physics shaped thinking for about two thousand years. He held that each of four elements, air, fire, water and earth, has its own natural place, with fire on top, then air, then water, then earth. So a fire burning on the ground sends its flames upward, back toward where fire belongs. He also taught that heavier objects fall faster, with speed in proportion to weight.

paragraphs.heading: Byzantium and the Islamic world
paragraphs.text: After the Western Roman Empire fell in the fifth century, learning declined in western Europe. In the east, the Byzantine Empire held out and kept advancing fields including physics. Islamic scholars took up Aristotle's physics and built on it during the Islamic Golden Age, above all in optics and vision. In his Book of Optics, Ibn al-Haytham proposed light rays in place of the ancient Greek idea of visual rays. He ran controlled experiments to confirm the laws of refraction and reflection using this new idea.

paragraphs.heading: Calculus and the modern laws
paragraphs.text: Newton, and separately Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz, created calculus, the mathematics of continuous change, and Newton used it to solve physical problems. During the Industrial Revolution, the growing need for energy drove research that uncovered laws of thermodynamics, chemistry and electromagnetics. As the 19th century closed, the theories of mechanics, thermodynamics and electromagnetics fit a broad range of observations.

paragraphs.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs.text: New ideas in physics often explain the basic workings that other sciences study, and they open new lines of research in fields as distant as mathematics and philosophy. Progress in physics also tends to make new technology possible. A better grasp of electromagnetism, solid-state physics and nuclear physics led straight to television, computers, household appliances and nuclear weapons. Work in thermodynamics fed industrialization, and work in mechanics helped inspire calculus.
